title: Stress and strain analysis
summary: The elastic constant relations E = 2G(1+μ) = 3K(1−2μ) and the principal stress equations are the two computational cores, and both are worth deriving once so they can be reconstructed. Beyond that, three ideas earn marks repeatedly: thermal stress arises only where a member is restrained, a sudden load produces twice the stress of a gradual one, and hoop stress in a thin cylinder is twice the longitudinal stress — which is why a pressure vessel splits along a longitudinal seam.

sections.heading: Stress, strain and the elastic constants
sections.body:
**Simple stress and strain:**

> **σ = P/A**,  **ε = δL/L**,  and by **Hooke's law** **σ = Eε**, hence **δL = PL/(AE)**

The product **AE** is the **axial rigidity**, the analogue of **EI** in bending and **GJ** in torsion.

**Poisson's ratio:**

> **μ = − lateral strain / longitudinal strain**

| Material | μ |
|---|---|
| Cork | ≈ 0 |
| **Concrete** | **0.15 – 0.20** |
| **Steel** | **≈ 0.30** |
| Aluminium | 0.33 |
| **Rubber** | **≈ 0.50** |

Its theoretical limits are **0 to 0.5**, and at exactly 0.5 the material is **incompressible** — which follows from the volumetric strain relation below.

**Volumetric strain** for a bar under uniaxial stress:

> **ε_v = ε(1 − 2μ)**

so when **μ = 0.5** the volume does not change at all. For a body under three mutually perpendicular stresses:

> **ε_v = (σ_x + σ_y + σ_z)(1 − 2μ)/E**

**The four elastic constants and their relations:**

> **E = 2G(1 + μ)**
> **E = 3K(1 − 2μ)**
> **E = 9KG/(3K + G)**

where **G** is the **modulus of rigidity (shear modulus)** and **K** the **bulk modulus**. Only **two** are independent for an isotropic material — given any two, the other two follow.

For steel with μ = 0.3: **G = E/2.6 ≈ 0.385E** and **K = E/1.2 ≈ 0.833E**. So

> **E > K > G** for ordinary metals

which is a quick sanity check on any computed value: a calculation giving G larger than E has gone wrong.

**The stress–strain curve for mild steel**, in order:

**proportional limit → elastic limit → upper yield point → lower yield point → strain hardening to the ultimate stress → necking → fracture**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **Proportional limit** | Where Hooke's law ceases; E is the slope up to here |
| **Elastic limit** | Slightly above; beyond it, some strain is permanent |
| **Yield point** | **Distinct in mild steel**; absent in high-strength steel and concrete |
| **Ultimate stress** | The maximum on the nominal-stress curve |
| **Breaking stress** | **Lower** than ultimate, because **necking** reduces the real area while nominal stress uses the original area |

The **breaking stress being below the ultimate** is a favourite question, and the reason is exactly that: on a **true** stress–strain curve (using the actual reduced area) the stress rises monotonically to fracture.

Because **high-strength steel and concrete show no distinct yield point**, a **0.2% proof stress** is used instead — the stress at which a permanent strain of 0.002 remains on unloading. That is why IS 1786 defines grades by "yield strength **or 0.2% proof stress**".

**Ductility, malleability, toughness, resilience** — the terms that questions swap:

| Property | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Ductility** | Can be drawn into **wire** — large plastic strain in tension |
| **Malleability** | Can be hammered into **sheets** — large plastic strain in compression |
| **Toughness** | **Total energy** absorbed to fracture — the whole area under the curve |
| **Resilience** | Energy absorbed **within the elastic range** |
| **Hardness** | Resistance to indentation and scratching |
| Brittleness | Fracture with little plastic strain |

sections.heading: Compound bars, thermal stress and strain energy
sections.body:
**Compound (composite) bars** — two materials sharing one load. The two governing conditions:

> **Equilibrium: P = P₁ + P₂**
> **Compatibility: δ₁ = δ₂**, hence **σ₁/E₁ = σ₂/E₂** for equal lengths

So the **stiffer material carries the greater stress**, in proportion to its modulus. That is the principle behind reinforced concrete: steel, with E about 15 times that of concrete, attracts a correspondingly larger share of the stress at the same strain — which is the origin of the **modular ratio m = E_s/E_c**.

**Thermal stress.** A free member expands by **δ = αLΔT** with **no stress whatever**. Stress arises **only if the expansion is restrained**:

> **Fully restrained: σ = α E ΔT**
> **Partially restrained (yield of supports δ_y): σ = E(αLΔT − δ_y)/L**

**This is the point of the topic:** thermal stress is a **restraint** phenomenon, not a temperature phenomenon. A long unrestrained pipe on rollers develops none; the same pipe anchored at both ends develops a great deal. Coefficient for steel **α ≈ 12 × 10⁻⁶ /°C**, for concrete **10 × 10⁻⁶**.

The practical consequences are everywhere: **expansion joints** in bridges, buildings and penstocks; **rail gaps**; expansion loops in pipelines; and **contraction joints** in concrete pavements — all provided so that movement occurs freely instead of generating stress.

For a **compound bar** under temperature change, the two materials have different α, so each restrains the other: the one that would expand more goes into **compression** and the other into **tension**, with equal and opposite forces.

**Strain energy.** The work done in straining a body elastically is stored and recoverable:

> **U = ½ P δ = σ²V/(2E)**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Resilience** | Total strain energy stored |
| **Proof resilience** | Strain energy at the **elastic limit** |
| **Modulus of resilience** | Proof resilience **per unit volume** |

**Loading types**, and this comparison is examined directly:

| Loading | Stress |
|---|---|
| **Gradual** | **σ = P/A** |
| **Sudden** | **σ = 2P/A** — **twice** the gradual value |
| **Impact** (load falling through h) | σ = (P/A)[1 + √(1 + 2AEh/(PL))] |

**A sudden load produces twice the stress of a gradually applied one**, and the reason is energy: the load descends through the full deflection while retaining its full value, so it does **twice** the work that a gradually increasing load would. Since the strain energy stored is ½σ²V/E — quadratic in stress — doubling the work doubles the stress. Understanding it this way makes the factor of 2 memorable rather than arbitrary.

For **impact**, the same reasoning with the extra potential energy Ph gives the bracketed expression; when h is large it approaches **σ = √(2PEh/(AL))**.

**Strain energy in the other modes**, for completeness:

| Mode | Strain energy |
|---|---|
| **Axial** | P²L/(2AE) |
| **Bending** | ∫M²dx/(2EI) |
| **Torsion** | T²L/(2GJ) |
| **Shear** | τ²V/(2G) |

The bending expression is the one used in **Castigliano's theorem** and the **unit load method** for deflections.

sections.heading: Principal stresses and Mohr's circle
sections.body:
For a two-dimensional stress state (σ_x, σ_y, τ):

> **σ₁,₂ = (σ_x + σ_y)/2 ± √[((σ_x − σ_y)/2)² + τ²]**
> **τ_max = √[((σ_x − σ_y)/2)² + τ²] = (σ₁ − σ₂)/2**
> **tan 2θ = 2τ/(σ_x − σ_y)**

**Four properties that answer most questions without calculation:**

1. **Shear stress is ZERO on a principal plane** — that is the definition of a principal plane.
2. The two principal planes are **90° apart**.
3. The planes of **maximum shear** are at **45° to the principal planes**.
4. **σ_x + σ_y is invariant** — it equals σ₁ + σ₂ whatever the orientation.

The fourth is a useful arithmetic check: if the computed principal stresses do not sum to the original normal stresses, the calculation is wrong.

**Mohr's circle** represents the same information graphically:

| Feature | Value |
|---|---|
| **Centre** | ((σ_x + σ_y)/2, 0) |
| **Radius** | **τ_max** |
| Intercepts on the σ axis | **σ₁ and σ₂** |
| Highest and lowest points | **± τ_max**, at σ = centre |

**The essential convention:** an angle **2θ** measured on the circle corresponds to **θ** on the physical element, and in the same sense. Forgetting the factor of two is the most common error in using it.

**Special cases worth knowing outright:**

| State | Principal stresses |
|---|---|
| **Uniaxial tension σ** | σ₁ = σ, σ₂ = 0; **τ_max = σ/2 at 45°** |
| **Pure shear τ** | **σ₁ = +τ, σ₂ = −τ**, at **45°** |
| Equal biaxial σ | σ₁ = σ₂ = σ; **circle degenerates to a point**, τ_max = 0 |
| Hydrostatic | Same in all directions; no shear on any plane |

**Uniaxial tension giving τ_max = σ/2 at 45°** explains why a mild steel bar in tension shows **Lüders bands at 45°** and why a ductile material fails in **shear** even under pure tension.

**Pure shear giving equal tension and compression at 45°** explains why a **brittle shaft in torsion fails on a 45° helix**: torsion is pure shear, the maximum tensile stress is on a 45° plane, and a brittle material fails in tension. A **ductile** shaft in the same torsion fails on a **transverse** plane, because it fails in shear instead. That contrast — same loading, different failure surface, according to the material — is a classic examination item.

**Theories of failure**, which apply the above to a design criterion:

| Theory | Criterion | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **Maximum principal stress (Rankine)** | σ₁ = σ_y | **Brittle** materials |
| **Maximum shear stress (Tresca / Guest)** | (σ₁ − σ₂)/2 = σ_y/2 | **Ductile**; conservative |
| **Maximum distortion energy (von Mises)** | Equivalent stress = σ_y | **Ductile**; the best agreement with test |
| Maximum principal strain (St Venant) | — | Rarely used |
| Maximum strain energy (Haigh) | — | Rarely used |

**Brittle materials by the principal stress theory, ductile by von Mises or Tresca** is the pairing to remember, and the reason follows from the failure surfaces above: brittle materials separate on the plane of maximum tension, ductile ones slip on the plane of maximum shear.

sections.heading: Thin cylinders and spheres
sections.body:
A vessel is treated as **thin** when **d/t > 20** (some texts use 15), so the stress may be taken as uniform through the wall thickness.

**Thin cylinder** under internal pressure p:

> **Circumferential (hoop) stress σ_h = pd/(2t)**
> **Longitudinal (axial) stress σ_l = pd/(4t)**

> **σ_h = 2 σ_l** — the hoop stress is **TWICE** the longitudinal

**Therefore a cylindrical vessel bursts along a LONGITUDINAL seam**, because the hoop stress acts **across** that seam and is the larger. This is the most examined single fact in the topic, and it is why a riveted boiler's longitudinal joint is made stronger (double riveted) than its circumferential joint.

Deriving them is quick and worth doing once. For hoop stress, consider a longitudinal section of length L: the bursting force is **p × d × L** and it is resisted by **σ_h × 2tL**, giving σ_h = pd/2t. For longitudinal stress, consider a transverse section: the force **p × πd²/4** is resisted by **σ_l × πdt**, giving σ_l = pd/4t.

**Thin sphere:**

> **σ = pd/(4t)** in **every** direction

A sphere carries **half the maximum stress of a cylinder** of the same diameter and thickness, which is why a **sphere is the most efficient pressure vessel** — and why high-pressure gas storage is spherical despite being more expensive to fabricate. The reason is geometric: a sphere's curvature resists the pressure equally in two directions at every point, while a cylinder resists it in only one.

**Strains and volumetric change** in a thin cylinder:

> **ε_h = (pd/2tE)(1 − μ/2)**
> **ε_l = (pd/2tE)(1/2 − μ)**
> **ε_v = (pd/2tE)(5/2 − 2μ)**

and for a sphere **ε_v = 3pd(1 − μ)/(4tE)**.

**Efficiency of a riveted joint** in a boiler shell:

> **η = strength of the joint / strength of the solid plate**

and the required thickness includes the joint efficiency: **t = pd/(2σ_allowable η)**.

**Thick cylinders** — where d/t is small — need **Lamé's theory**, because the hoop stress then varies substantially through the wall, being **maximum at the inner surface**:

> **σ_h = b/r² + a**,  **σ_r = b/r² − a**

The practical consequence is that simply increasing the wall thickness of a thick cylinder gives diminishing returns, since the added material near the outside is lightly stressed. That is why very high pressure vessels are made as **compound cylinders**, one shrunk onto another to pre-compress the inner one, or are **autofrettaged** — deliberately overstrained so that residual compression remains at the bore.

**Where thin-cylinder theory is used in civil engineering:** **penstocks and pressure pipes** (where the water hammer pressure, not the static head, usually governs the thickness), **water tanks**, **hoop stress in a circular water-retaining wall**, and **prestressing wire wound around a circular tank** — the last being a direct application of hoop tension, where the winding supplies the tension the concrete cannot.

formulas.label: Hooke's law and axial deformation
formulas.note: AE is the axial rigidity, analogous to EI in bending and GJ in torsion.

formulas.label: Elastic constant relations
formulas.note: Only two are independent. For steel (μ = 0.3): G ≈ 0.385E, K ≈ 0.833E, so E > K > G.

formulas.label: Volumetric strain
formulas.note: At μ = 0.5 the material is incompressible — the upper theoretical limit.

formulas.label: Thermal stress
formulas.expression: fully restrained σ = αEΔT ;   with support yield δ_y: σ = E(αLΔT − δ_y)/L
formulas.note: Arises ONLY where restrained. A free member expands with no stress at all. Steel α ≈ 12 × 10⁻⁶/°C.

formulas.label: Strain energy and loading type
formulas.expression: U = ½Pδ = σ²V/2E ;   gradual σ = P/A ;   SUDDEN σ = 2P/A ;   impact σ = (P/A)[1 + √(1 + 2AEh/PL)]
formulas.note: A sudden load does twice the work of a gradual one, hence twice the stress.

formulas.label: Principal stresses
formulas.note: Shear is zero on a principal plane; planes of max shear lie at 45° to them; σ_x + σ_y is invariant.

formulas.label: Pure shear and uniaxial tension
formulas.expression: Pure shear τ: σ₁ = +τ, σ₂ = −τ at 45°.   Uniaxial σ: τ_max = σ/2 at 45°.
formulas.note: Why a brittle shaft in torsion fails on a 45° helix and a ductile one on a transverse plane.

formulas.label: Thin cylinder
formulas.expression: hoop σ_h = pd/(2t) ;   longitudinal σ_l = pd/(4t) ;   σ_h = 2σ_l
formulas.note: So a cylinder bursts along a LONGITUDINAL seam. Thin means d/t > 20.

formulas.label: Thin sphere
formulas.note: Half the maximum stress of a cylinder — the sphere is the most efficient pressure vessel.
